query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting single‐phase ZrB2 with a high‐entropy diboride—by alloying ZrB2 with additional refractory diboride constituents (for example, forming an equimolar (Hf,Zr,Ta,Nb,Ti)B2)—will enable densification at reduced sintering temperatures (≤1700 °C) while simultaneously improving mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 that typically requires processing above 2300 °C but, when produced at lower temperatures, shows inferior oxidation durability and vulnerability to liquid metal corrosion.
generation.intervention: Modify the composition by introducing refractory diboride constituents (e.g., HfB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2) to form a single-phase, high-entropy diboride using spark plasma sintering at lower temperatures (≤1700 °C).
generation.conditions: Fabrication by spark plasma sintering at ≤1700 °C and subsequent service in high-temperature environments subject to oxidation and liquid metal (plating bath) corrosion.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a uniform high-entropy solid solution microstructure with increased lattice distortion and a more homogeneous grain-boundary network.
generation.mechanism: The added refractory elements promote activated sintering at lower temperatures, leading to enhanced densification and the development of a more cohesive microstructure. This high-entropy state reduces the formation of deleterious phases during processing and leads to the formation of a protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, which in turn improves both oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples processed as high-entropy diborides at ≤1700 °C will exhibit densification and mechanical strength comparable to or better than conventional ZrB2 fabricated at >2300 °C. They will also show improved oxidation resistance and stability in liquid plating metal environments.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of single-phase ZrB2 processed at >2300 °C and of lower-temperature fabricated ZrB2 variants that suffer from rapid oxidation and corrosion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the sintering is carried out at temperatures at or below 1700 °C and the resulting material is exposed to high-temperature oxidative conditions and corrosive liquid metal baths.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in toughness, oxidation kinetics, and long-term corrosion behavior require further investigation, especially under cyclic thermal loads and prolonged service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize samples of the equimolar high-entropy diboride (e.g., (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2) using spark plasma sintering at ≤1700 °C. Prepare control samples of conventional single-phase ZrB2 fabricated above 2300 °C and lower-temperature ZrB2 made without alloying additions. Characterize the phases (using XRD), microstructure (using SEM/TEM), and density. Then evaluate mechanical properties (Vickers hardness, compressive/tensile strength) and perform oxidation tests (weight gain, phase evolution) as well as liquid metal corrosion tests under simulated plating bath conditions.
measurements: Oxidation kinetics (weight gain and oxide scale analysis) at high temperatures
Corrosion resistance in a liquid plating metal environment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy diboride samples processed at ≤1700 °C do not achieve comparable or enhanced densification, mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and corrosion durability relative to conventional ZrB2 or if a multiphase structure forms, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Hardness and oxidation measurements were conducted using all six single-phase high-entropy diborides (HEB #1-#5 and #7) and six individual metal diboride benchmarking specimens (HfB2, ZrB2, TaB2, NbB2, TiB2, and CrB2) that were made by the same HEBM and SPS fabrication method using the same processing parameters, with one exception that CrB2 was sintered at lower temperature of 1800 °C because its substantially lower melting (and therefore sintering) temperature. MoB2 was not examined because it is not a thermodynamically stable phase (and will decompose to MoB and Mo2B5) below 1500 °C. Hardness measurements were performed with a Vickers’ diamond indenter at 200 kgf/mm2 with a hold time of 15 seconds. The indentations were examined for conformation with the ASTM C1327. The indentations averaged 20–25 μm in width during the testing. Multiple measurements were performed at different locations of each specimen; the mean and standard deviation are reported.
